title: Consonants
subtitle: C always hard, G complex, H guttural — the sounds modern English has lost.
objectives: Pronounce c as [k] before back vowels and as [tʃ] before front vowels.
Distinguish the three values of g: stop [ɡ], fricative [ɣ], palatal [j].
Produce the guttural h [x] as in German 'ach' or Scottish 'loch.'
Recognize and pronounce the consonant clusters sc, cg, ng.

sections.heading: C — hard and soft
sections.body:
The letter c in Old English represents two sounds, conditioned by the following vowel. Before back vowels (a, o, u) and before consonants, c is always [k] as in 'cat' or 'king.' Before front vowels (e, i, y) and before the diphthongs that begin with e or i, c is palatalized to [tʃ] as in 'church.'

Examples: cū (cow) — hard [k]. cild (child) — soft [tʃ]. cyning (king) — soft [tʃ]. ceaster (city, fort) — soft [tʃ].

This is not a spelling convention; it is a phonological rule. The Anglo-Saxons heard these as the same underlying sound in different environments. Modern English preserves some of these palatalizations (child, church, cheese) but has lost the rule.

sections.heading: G — stop, fricative, palatal
sections.body:
The letter g is more complex than c. It represents three sounds:

1. Stop [ɡ] — at the beginning of a word before a back vowel (a, o, u), and after n. Examples: gōd (good), gān (to go), gang (going), engel (angel).

2. Fricative [ɣ] — between vowels, and sometimes at the end of a word. This is the sound you hear in Spanish 'lago' or modern Greek γάλα. The back of the tongue approaches the soft palate but does not close fully. Examples: sorga (sorrow), daga (of days), boga (bow).

3. Palatal [j] — before or after front vowels (e, i, y) and before or after front diphthongs. This is the sound of modern English 'yes.' Examples: geong (young), gieldan (to pay), dæg (day), weg (way).

The same letter, three sounds, all predictable from context.

sections.heading: H — aspirate and guttural
sections.body:
Before a vowel, h is a simple aspirate [h] as in modern English 'house.' Before a consonant or at the end of a word, h is a voiceless velar fricative [x], the sound in German 'ach' or Scottish 'loch.' This sound does not exist in standard modern English, but it was common in Old English.

Examples: hūs (house) — aspirate [h]. niht (night) — guttural [x]. þurh (through) — guttural [x]. eahta (eight) — guttural [x] before t.

sections.heading: Consonant clusters
sections.body:
Three clusters require attention:

sc — before a back vowel, [sk] as in 'skill.' Before a front vowel, palatalized to [ʃ] as in 'ship.' Examples: scip (ship) — [ʃ]. sceadu (shadow) — [ʃ]. scolu (school) — [sk].

cg — after a front vowel, palatalized to [dʒ] as in 'judge.' Examples: ecg (edge), brycg (bridge), secgan (to say).

ng — always [ŋɡ] (as in 'finger'), never [ŋ] alone (as in 'sing'). Examples: lang (long), engel (angel), singan (to sing).

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Pronounce each word and identify the sound of the highlighted consonant.

items.prompt: Why does c have two sounds?
items.answer: Palatalization before front vowels. The Anglo-Saxons heard it as one phoneme in two environments.

sections.heading: Words with consonant complexity
sections.instructions: Listen and repeat. Pay attention to c, g, h, and clusters.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 1.5 covers stress and word accent. Old English stress falls almost always on the root syllable, not on prefixes or suffixes.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can pronounce c, g, and h correctly in ten different words.
